entries.html:
/veˈni.re/

Verb

  1. to come
  2. to arrive
    1. Synonyms: arrivare, giungere, sopraggiungere, manifestarsi, procedere, avvicinarsi, appressarsi, approssimarsi
  3. to manifest itself
    1. Synonyms: colpire, prendersi, beccarsi
  4. to take position
  5. to originate [with da ‘from’]
    1. Synonyms: provenire, derivare, discendere
  6. (vulgar, slang) to ejaculate; to cum
    1. Synonyms: godere, eiaculare, sborrare
  7. to come to mind
    1. Synonym: sovvenire
  8. to result
    1. Synonyms: risultare, avere esito
  9. to complete or be able to accomplish
    1. Synonyms: riuscire, risultare, avere esito, ottenere
  10. (informal) to cost
    1. Synonym: costare
  11. to be compelled (to); to have an impulse (to) [with da (+ infinitive) or di (+ infinitive)]
  12. to get, be (strictly for passive voice, see usage notes)
    1. Synonym: essere
  13. to be born (of a person)
    1. Synonym: nascere
  14. to come out of the ground; to spring up (of a plant)
    1. Synonyms: nascere, sorgere, crescere, spuntare, svilupparsi, attecchire
  15. to complete successfully; to come out; to end up

Usage Note

  1. It may be used as an auxiliary instead of essere for passive voice, but not in compound tenses.

Inherited from Latin venīre.

/ˈfa.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to do
  2. (transitive) to make
    1. to create
    2. to bring about
    3. to behave or act [with da ‘as’]
    4. to constitute
    5. to numerically result in; to add up to
    6. to formulate in the mind
    7. to cause to be; to render
    8. (ditransitive) to compel
    9. (ditransitive) to force
  3. to provoke (a physical sensation)
  4. (transitive) to inflict (damage, pain, etc.) on
  5. (transitive) to cause or arouse (an emotion)
  6. (transitive) to draw up or enter into (a contract, agreement, etc.)
  7. (transitive) to emit from the body
  8. (transitive) to have (a baby)
  9. (transitive) to produce a lot of (fruit or flowers) (of a plant)
  10. (transitive) to have (a certain population) (of a state, country, etc.)
  11. (transitive, informal) to cost
    1. to sell [with a ‘for (a price)’]
  12. (transitive) to clean up
  13. (transitive) to address
  14. (transitive) to organize or celebrate (an event, party, etc.)
  15. (transitive) to stage (a play, movie, etc.)
    1. to produce or participate in (a play, movie, etc.) (of a director, actor, etc.)
    2. to interpret (a role, character, etc.); to act
    3. to be planned or scheduled (at a certain time) [with a or in] (of a movie, show, etc., chiefly in the form fanno)
  16. (transitive) to be subscribed to; to do regularly
    1. to attend (a school), to be in (a grade level)
    2. to practice (a hobby, sport, etc.)
  17. (transitive) to follow (a road, etc.)
  18. (transitive) to visit (a country, city, etc.)
  19. (transitive) to last (an amount of time)
    1. (transitive, informal) to turn (an age)
  20. (transitive, informal) to gift
  21. (transitive) to tell or indicate (the time)
  22. (transitive) to do until (a time, typically at night)
  23. (transitive) to caricature
  24. (transitive) to spend; to pass (of time)
  25. (transitive) to live or lead (a kind of life)
  26. (transitive) to pronounce, judge, or evaluate
  27. (transitive) (with che + subj.) to suppose or consider
  28. (transitive) to gather
    1. (transitive) to stock up on
  29. (transitive) to work as (a profession)
  30. (transitive) to elect or nominate
  31. (transitive, sports, card games) to score
  32. (transitive) to make appear
    1. to create impressions of
  33. (transitive) (with inf.) to let
  34. (transitive) (with [di + inf.] or [che + subj.]) to strive or endeavor
  35. (intransitive) to be suitable [with per ‘for’] [auxiliary avere]
  36. (intransitive) to play [with a] [auxiliary avere]
  37. (intransitive) to be spent or to have gone by; to mark [auxiliary avere] (of time)
  38. (intransitive, impersonal) to be (hot, cold, etc.) [auxiliary avere] (of the weather, climate, etc.)
  39. (intransitive, grammar) to have as an inflected form [auxiliary avere] (of a word)
  40. (intransitive) to go (to say something or make a sound) [auxiliary avere]
  41. (intransitive) to go (to be expressed or composed) [auxiliary avere]
  42. (intransitive) to be formed by a sequence [auxiliary avere]
  43. (intransitive, with come (“how”)) to be able to [with a (+ infinitive); or with per (+ infinitive)] [auxiliary avere]
  44. (intransitive, rare) to take root [auxiliary avere] (of a plant)
  45. (intransitive, rare) to suffice [auxiliary avere] (of a plant)

Noun m.

  1. manner, way

Usage Note

  1. fa' + mi = fammi
    1. ... + lo = fammelo
    2. ... + la = fammela
    3. ... + le = fammele
    4. ... + li = fammeli
    5. ... + ne = fammene
  2. fa' + ti = fatti
    1. ... + lo = fattelo
    2. ... + la = fattela
    3. ... + le = fattele
    4. ... + li = fatteli
    5. ... + ne = fattene
  3. fa' + gli = fagli and fa' + le = falle
    1. ... + lo = faglielo
    2. ... + la = fagliela
    3. ... + le = fagliele
    4. ... + li = faglieli
    5. ... + ne = fagliene
  4. fa' + ci = facci
    1. ... + lo = faccelo
    2. ... + la = faccela
    3. ... + le = faccele
    4. ... + li = facceli
    5. ... + ne = faccene
  5. fa' + lo = fallo
  6. fa' + la = falla
  7. fa' + le = falle
  8. fa' + li = falli
  9. fa' + ne = fanne

Inherited from Late Latin fāre.

/veˈde.re/

Verb

  1. to see
  2. to look at
  3. to meet
  4. to visit
  5. to grasp (an idea)
  6. to make sure [with di (+ infinitive) ‘to do something’] (otherwise, there will be a negative consequence)

Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *weyd-.

/troˈva.re/

Verb

  1. to find
  2. (informal) to visit (a friend, relative, etc.)
  3. to contact or get hold of (someone)
  4. to come by; to come across
  5. to think; to believe; also [with che (+ subjunctive clause)]
  6. to think up
  7. (archaic or literary) to compose poetry

Synonym

  1. scorgere
  2. incontrare
  3. ottenere
  4. avere
  5. riconoscere

Usage Note

  1. Often used with da, followed by an infinitive, to imply place. For instance:

From Vulgar Latin *tropāre, a verb probably based on Classical Latin tropus. Compare French trouver.

Borrowed from Old Occitan trobar, from Vulgar Latin *tropāre, from Latin tropus.

/anˈda.re/

Verb

  1. to go [auxiliary essere]
  2. (intransitive, impersonal, third person only) to be agreeable (to), to be pleasing (to) (idiomatically, to feel like, to want/like) [with a and di ‘thing desired’] [auxiliary essere]
  3. to attend (school, church regularly) [with a]
  4. (auxiliary) used to form the passive voice with a connotation of obligation or prescription
  5. to enter, to take on, to experience [with in ‘a condition, emotion, etc.’] [auxiliary essere]

Usage Note

  1. Unlike Spanish ir a, Portuguese ir, and French aller, this verb is not used as auxiliary for a future periphrasis with the infinitive.

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin, with suppletion from vādō.

/koˈnja.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to mint (coinage)
  2. (transitive) to strike (medals)
  3. (transitive) to coin (words)

From conio +‎ -are.

/sor.monˈta.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to overcome or surmount; to be on top of something
  2. (intransitive) to overlap [with con] [auxiliary essere]

Borrowed from Old French sormonter. First attested in the 14th century. By surface analysis, sor- +‎ montare.

/in.ɡloˈba.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to include or incorporate (external elements) into a unified whole
  2. (transitive) to embed

From in- +‎ globo +‎ -are.

/ri.belˈla.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive, archaic, rare) to incite, to cause to rebel

From Latin rebellāre.

/ˈɛs.se.re/

Verb

  1. (copulative) Used as a copula. to be
  2. Denotes absolute time.
  3. (auxiliary) Used with as an auxiliary in the conjugation of other verbs, before their past participle.
    1. Forms composite forms of some intransitive verbs. See the full list.
    2. Forms composite forms for passive voice for all verbs.
    3. Forms composite forms for reflexive voice for all verbs
  4. (intransitive) to exist, there be
    1. Most commonly with ci or vi, see the appropriate entries at esserci and esservi for more information.
    2. (archaic) Without any clitics.
  5. (intransitive) to be real
  6. (intransitive) to happen, occur; to be
  7. (intransitive) to cost
    1. Synonyms: (both more common in questions) costare, venire
  8. Denotes spatial and temporal distance.
  9. (intransitive, literary) to live, be alive
  10. (intransitive, dated) to be about to [with per (+ infinitive)]
    1. Synonym: stare

Noun m.

  1. (uncountable, substantival use of the verbal voice, the condition of have life, reality, existence, the act of be living) being, living
    1. Synonyms: essenza, esistere, esistenza
  2. (countable, substantival use of the verbal voice, the condition of have life, reality, existence, the act of be living) being, living
    1. Synonym: (more common) vivere
  3. (uncountable, substantival use of the verbal voice, the act/fact of exist, existence, life) being
    1. Synonyms: (countable) esistenza, (countable) vita
  4. (uncountable, way of being, condition, state, in relation to intrinsic qualities and properties, usually accompanied by a determination) being
    1. Synonyms: modo di essere, condizione, stato, essenza
  5. (uncountable, in ancient phrases) being; living; existence; condition
  6. (uncountable, in ancient phrases) being, condition
    1. Synonym: (countable) condizione
  7. (uncountable, in ancient phrases) being, in good conditions
    1. Synonym: buone condizioni
  8. (uncountable, in ancient phrases) ready
    1. Synonym: (countable) pronto
  9. (uncountable, in ancient phrases) place, operation
    1. Synonym: (uncountable) esercizio
  10. (uncountable, concrete) being
  11. (countable, concrete) being, creature
  12. (countable, concrete, by extension) living being, creature
    1. Synonyms: essere vivente, creatura
  13. (uncountable, philosophy, followed by ci) existence
    1. Synonym: esistenza

Conjugation

  1. Truncated apocopic forms exist for many of the above forms:

Usage Note

  1. The present participle essente is very rare, and is usually replaced with stante, the present participle of stare, or with the present participles of its synonyms. Similarly the past participle essuto has disappeared, with stato, the past participle of stare, being used instead.
  2. The verb essere, including all of its conjugated forms, is the word that occurs most frequently in speech.
  3. When stating an amount, for example amount of money to pay for a service, Italian, unlike English, uses the third plural sono, not third singular è.

Inherited from Latin sum, esse. The infinitive form is attested already from Early Medieval Latin essere. The past participle stato, shared with the verb stare, is from Latin stātus.

/aˈve.re/ · /havere/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to have
    1. Synonyms: possedere, (regional) tenere
  2. (auxiliary, the non-perfect forms followed by the masculine singular past participle, used to form composite (perfect) tenses in the active and dative conjugations of the transitive verbs) to have (done something); See Category:Italian transitive verbs and Category:Italian reflexive verbs.
  3. (impersonal, obsolete and Tuscan, or literary) synonym of esserci: there be

Noun m.

  1. property, substance
  2. (in the plural) belongings
  3. assets
  4. swag
  5. credit

Usage Note

  1. sense 3 is, as is French y avoir, only found in the singular.

Inherited from Latin habēre.

/poˈte.re/

Verb

  1. (ambitransitive) can, could; to be able to
  2. (ambitransitive) may, might; to be possible to

Noun m.

  1. power

Usage Note

  1. This verb is not used with verbs relating to the senses: Lo vedo. (“I (can) see it.”) Non lo sento. (“I can't / don't feel it.”) However, riuscire can be used in such contexts if one wants to stress the effort made: Non riesco a vederlo. (“I can't see it (much as I try).”)

Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

/doˈve.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to owe
  2. (auxiliary) to have to do something (must)

Noun m.

  1. duty

Interjection

  1. Dismisses gratitude by clarifying one acted for one's duty rather than for kindness.

Usage Note

  1. As an auxiliary, dovere takes avere or essere, depending on the verb that follows it.
  2. All conditional forms, like dovrei, are translated as should.

Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.

/ˈda.re/

Verb

  1. to give (to transfer the possession/holding of something to someone else)
  2. to yield, to bear, to produce, to return
  3. (ditransitive) to name, to call, to refer to [with del ‘as’, along with a or a dative pronoun ‘to (someone)’]
  4. (transitive, vulgar, slang) chiefly in the form darla: acquiesce to a sexual intercourse

Noun m.

  1. debit

Usage Note

  1. It is customary to write a grave accent on some forms of the indicative present, to distinguish them from homographs:
    1. optionally dò (I give), contrasting with do (“C musical note”)
    2. rarely dài (you give), contrasting with dai (“from the”)
    3. compulsory dà (he/she/it gives), contrasting with da (“from”)
    4. rarely dànno (they give), contrasting with danno (damage)
  2. The imperative forms of the second-person singular are compounded with pronouns as follows:
    1. da' + ci → dacci
      1. ... + lo → daccelo
      2. ... + la → dacceli
      3. ... + le → daccele
      4. ... + ne → daccene
    2. da' + gli → dagli
    3. da' + gli/le + la → dagliela
    4. da' + gli/le + le → dagliele
    5. da' + gli/le + li → daglieli
    6. da' + gli/le + lo → daglielo
    7. da' + gli/le + ne → dagliene
    8. da' + le → dalle
    9. da' + mi → dammi
      1. ... + lo → dammelo
      2. ... + la → dammeli
      3. ... + le → dammele
      4. ... + ne → dammene

Inherited from Latin dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).

/voˈle.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive, modal) to want

Noun m.

  1. will, wish, desire, want
    1. Synonym: volontà

Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

/porˈta.re/

Verb

  1. to bring, fetch, take, carry
  2. (figurative, by extension) to transmit; to relay
  3. to propose
    1. Synonyms: proporre, candidare, designare
  4. to lead or drive
    1. Synonyms: condurre, menare, convogliare, dirigere, guidare
  5. to wear
    1. Synonyms: avere, indossare, calzare, avere indosso, usare, mettere
  6. to bear; to feel; to harbor (of a feeling)
    1. Synonyms: provare, nutrire, serbare, conservare

Inherited from Latin portāre (“to bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).

/ˈprɛn.de.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to take, hold, pick up, get
    1. Synonyms: tenere, agguantare, stringere, afferrare, impugnare, brandire, ghermire, pigliare
  2. (transitive) to conquer (of a political territory or entity)
    1. Synonyms: conquistare, occupare, espugnare
  3. (transitive) to take (a means of transport)
  4. (transitive, by extension) to choose (a certain route or path)
    1. Synonyms: immettersi, incanalarsi, infilare, avviarsi, affacciarsi
  5. (transitive) to catch (a criminal, animal, etc.)
    1. Synonyms: catturare, arrestare, acchiappare, acciuffare
  6. (transitive, by extension) to catch (an illness)
    1. Synonym: contrarre
  7. (informal, transitive) to be beat up or defeated
    1. Synonym: prenderle
  8. (transitive) to get, buy
    1. Synonyms: acquistare, comprare, comperare, procurarsi
  9. (transitive, informal) to steal
    1. Synonyms: sgraffignare, derubare, fregare
  10. (transitive) to assume (a task, responsibility, etc.)
    1. Synonym: assumere
  11. (transitive) to hit or strike
    1. Synonyms: colpire, battere, percuotere, ferire, danneggiare, ledere
    2. (of a target) Synonyms: colpire, azzeccare, imbroccare
  12. (transitive) to hit or strike [with a ‘with/using’]
  13. (transitive) to eat, drink, ingest (of food, drink, medicine, etc.)
    1. Synonyms: ingerire, assumere, bere, mangiare, servirsi
  14. (transitive, informal) to romantically attract
    1. Synonyms: attirare, attrarre, conquistare, stregare, innamorare, abbagliare, incantare, sedurre, allettare, ammaliare, rapire, estasiare
  15. (transitive) to acquire (a characteristic)
    1. Synonyms: ereditare, derivare, acquisire
  16. (transitive) to pursue (a vocation)
  17. (transitive) to measure
  18. (transitive) to pick up, receive (a radio, TV, telegraphic, etc. transmission)
    1. Synonyms: captare, ricevere
  19. (transitive) to feel (an emotion)
  20. (transitive) to take hold of, seize, or strike (someone) (of a sensation, feeling, etc.)
  21. (transitive, informal) to occupy or take up (space or time)
    1. Synonym: occupare
  22. (transitive, informal, by extension) to occupy someone's mind
  23. (transitive) to require (energy, effort, etc.)
  24. (transitive) (sometimes with per) to take for or confuse
    1. Synonyms: scambiare, confondere, credere, ritenere
  25. (transitive) to interpret
    1. Synonyms: interpretare, intendere, scegliere, adottare
  26. (transitive) to choose (someone for a role, job, etc.); to hire
  27. (transitive) to treat (someone) (in a certain way)
  28. (transitive) to accept
  29. (intransitive) (with a or per) to move (towards); to head (for) [auxiliary avere]
  30. (intransitive) (with a + inf.) to begin [auxiliary avere]
  31. (intransitive) to begin to burn [auxiliary avere] (of a fire)
    1. Synonym: appiccare
  32. (construction, intransitive) to adhere to the building materials by hardening; to take hold [auxiliary avere] (of a binder)
    1. Synonyms: attaccare, indurire, fare presa, solidificarsi
  33. (intransitive) to take root [auxiliary avere] (of a plant)
  34. (intransitive) to happen unexpectedly [auxiliary essere or avere]
    1. Synonyms: capitare, accadere, sopraggiungere
  35. (vulgar, slang) in the form "prenderlo", literally "to take it": to be penetrated sexually

Inherited from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendere (“take, seize”) (not attested without a prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

/ri.uʃˈʃi.re/

Verb

  1. to manage; to be able [with a or di (+ infinitive) ‘to do something’]
    1. Synonyms: essere capace, essere in grado di, essere all'altezza, potere
  2. to be able to be accomplished [with a ‘by someone’, along with a or di (+ infinitive) ‘to do something’] (idiomatically translated as English be able with subject and object reversed)
  3. to end up or turn out [with bene ‘well’, male ‘badly’, etc.]
  4. to reach (a position, qualification, etc.); to become
  5. to achieve (a certain position in standings)
  6. to succeed; to do well [with in ‘in something’]
    1. Synonyms: avere successo, ottenere, conseguire, farcela, spuntarla, vincere, arrivare
  7. (copulative) to appear [with a (+ predicative adjective) ‘in some state’]
    1. Synonyms: dimostrarsi, sembrare, apparire, rivelarsi
  8. to exit or go out again
    1. Synonyms: uscire di nuovo, andarsene
  9. to exit [with da ‘from a different place than the entrance’]
  10. to continue after a break or obstacle (of a pathway, road, etc.) [with su ‘on/in some location’]
    1. Synonyms: sboccare, giungere, andare a finire, pervenire

Usage Note

  1. (be able to): Typically phrased using the active voice, but (as illustrated in the third example) the passive voice, with the agent followed by a or represented using an indirect object pronoun.
  2. (turn out): When not followed by a complement, implies that the given item, action, etc. turned out well.

From ri- +‎ uscire. Compare French réussir, borrowed via riuscita.

/uˈza.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to use
  2. (transitive) to do (a courtesy, a favor)
  3. (transitive) to exercise (a right)
  4. (transitive) to be accustomed to, to be used to (doing something) (+ infinitive)
  5. (intransitive) to make use [with di ‘of’] [auxiliary avere]
  6. (intransitive) to be in use, to be fashionable [auxiliary avere]
  7. (intransitive, literary) to be familiar [with con ‘with’] [auxiliary avere]
  8. (intransitive, impersonal, uncommon) to be customary [auxiliary essere]

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre. Cognate with French user.

/u.ti.lidˈd͡za.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to use, make use of, utilize

From utile +‎ -izzare.

/i.nitˈt͡sja.re/

Verb

  1. (ambitransitive) to begin, to set about
  2. to join, to incorporate

Synonym

  1. cominciare, incominciare

Borrowed from Latin initiāre. Cf. also cominciare.

/ri.maˈne.re/

Verb

  1. to stay
  2. to remain
  3. to be left

Synonym

  1. restare
  2. trovarsi

From Latin remanēre, from re- + maneō.

/ˈmet.te.re/

Verb

  1. (transitive) to put, to place, to lay, to set
    1. Synonym: porre
  2. (transitive) to deposit
  3. (transitive) to bet, to wager
  4. (transitive) to cut (new teeth)
  5. (transitive) to lead (someone) to, to provoke in (someone), to make (someone) feel [with a or in ‘a certain condition or state of mind’]
  6. (transitive, colloquial) to charge (an amount of money)
  7. (transitive) to don, to put on
  8. (intransitive) to give, to lead onto (of a street, road, etc.) [auxiliary avere]
  9. (intransitive) to bud, to develop (of plants) [auxiliary avere]
  10. (intransitive) to turn out (well or badly) [auxiliary avere]
  11. (intransitive, vulgar, slang) in the form "metterlo", literally "to put it": to penetrate sexually
  12. (intransitive, vulgar, slang) in the form "metterlo", literally "to put it": to cheat, to swindle, to scam

Inherited from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French mettre, Spanish meter, Occitan metre, and English mission.

/pub.bliˈka.re/

Verb

  1. to publish

From Latin pūblicāre.

/ar.riˈva.re/

Verb

  1. (intransitive) to arrive, to come, to reach [auxiliary essere]
    1. Synonyms: giungere, pervenire
  2. (intransitive, sports) to come, to be placed [auxiliary essere]
  3. (transitive, literary) to reach (a person) [auxiliary avere]

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre, perhaps influenced from Gallo-Italic or Old French in comparison to arripare. By surface analysis, a- +‎ riva (“shore”) +‎ -are.

/di.venˈta.re/

Verb

  1. to become (rich, dry, a doctor, etc.), to go (crazy, etc.), to turn (red, blue, etc.)
    1. Synonym: divenire

From a verbal derivative of Latin dēventum, perfect passive participle of dēveniō (“arrive, come”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *dēventāre as a frequentative of this verb.

/ˈskri.ve.re/

Verb

  1. (ambitransitive) to write [auxiliary avere]
  2. (transitive) to spell (to write the letters that form (a word))
  3. (transitive) to write down

/kjaˈma.re/

/ot.teˈne.re/

/pre.zenˈta.re/

/laʃˈʃa.re/

/parˈla.re/

/ˈnaʃ.ʃe.re/

/seˈɡwi.re/

/enˈtra.re/

/kor.reˈla.re/
